description:
We're a young team of gamers and tech enthusiasts from Uberlândia, Brazil!

Our mission is to build a fun, interactive space survival game that helps young astronauts learn about real NASA missions through challenges, decisions, and resource management.

We love gaming, technology, creative ideas, and experimenting with AI. We're here to learn, build something cool, and have a great time along the way!
summary: MARS OPS: Last Outpost is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12 that trains junior astronauts to run a small base on Mars, one sol (Martian day) at a time. Players walk around the base, answer alerts in each building and split the day's solar power between air, food, science and a radiation shield. Every choice has a cost, now or later, so kids learn that space missions are about trade-offs. Real space weather drives the story: solar flares, plasma clouds and geomagnetic storms from NASA's DONKI database become radio alerts from Mission Control, with the real date and a link to the NASA record. When something goes wrong there is no game over: Mission Control explains what happened and kids can go back to an earlier sol and try a different plan. The game runs on phones and computers, needs no login, collects no personal data and is available in English, Portuguese, Spanish, French and Italian, with music, sound effects and voiced characters.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MARS OPS: Last Outpost is a mission trainer game for children aged 7 to 12. The player commands a small Mars base for 7 or 10 sols (three difficulty levels). Each sol:

- Alerts appear on buildings (air factory, greenhouse, lab, antenna, shelter, solar panels, rover). The child walks there, uses the terminal and picks one of two choices. Every choice has a cost: air, food, health, power or science, now or on a later sol (marked with an hourglass). A "Why?" button explains the science in one or two sentences.

- The child splits the day's solar power between the air factory, the greenhouse, the lab (science, which earns 1 to 3 stars) and a sand shield that reduces radiation.

- A clock runs through the day. If night comes before the crew goes to bed, they get tired. Unanswered alerts get worse on their own.

- A night report shows what was produced, consumed and lost.

If air, food or health runs out, Earth rescues the crew. There is no game over: a mission report shows which decisions mattered and lets the child return to an earlier sol and try again.

NASA DATA

Solar flares (FLR), coronal mass ejections (CME), solar energetic particle events (SEP) and geomagnetic storms (GST) come from NASA's DONKI space weather database (CCMC), fetched live in the browser with no API key, with a verified archive as a fallback. Each solar card shows the real date, a "live" or "archived" badge and a link to the NASA record. The radio delay between Earth and Mars shown on each message is computed from NASA/JPL approximate planetary positions. Events also reference real missions and facts (Perseverance and MOXIE, Curiosity RAD, InSight, Ingenuity, ISS life support). Everything invented for gameplay (the base, the robot Rovi, the energy numbers) is labeled as such on the "Sources" page and in the "What is real?" help page.

DESIGN FOR KIDS

Short sentences with science words explained in the same sentence; a guided first sol with arrows; a robot helper that warns when air or food is dropping and says what to do; five languages; works on phones and computers (touch targets of 44 px or more); no login, no ads, no tracking, progress saved only in the browser; sound and voices can be adjusted or turned off.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React 19, TanStack Start, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Vitest (45 automated tests, plus simulations of thousands of missions to tune difficulty), deployed on Vercel. Built with Lovable, Claude Code and ChatGPT/Codex. Pixel art with AI image tools edited by the team, music with Suno, voices and ambience with ElevenLabs, 8-bit effects synthesized by code.

CREATIVITY

Real NASA space weather turns into story events in a kid-friendly survival game, and failure becomes a lesson instead of a game over.
